blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
THE POWER OF HOLY GHOST CONVICTION
Scripture Text: Acts 9:1-9

Last week we studied of the salvation of one individual— the eunuch from Africa. God used a man to reach him, and it seemed such an easy task. Today we study another individual in his move to Christ. God used a miraculous vision from Heaven and physical means to reach Saul of Tarsus, or Paul. This seemed a more difficult task.

This quarter we go on with our study of the early church as told in Acts. The evidence found here of the power of God to change lives and use those lives to His glory should move us to seek that same power. God gave us this history to excite like action. He put this picture before us to show how He will use us also. No one can do this in his own strength. We must do it as these saints of Acts did it—by the power of the Holy Spirit, under His direction.
MEMORY VERSE: And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do. —Acts 9:6
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Acts 26:1-20 Paul's testimony.
Tue.—Philippians 2:1-16 Giving up all for Christ.
Wed.—Galatians 1:11-17 Paul's authority of divine origin.
Thu.—1 Timothy 1:1-11 Glorious Gospel committed to Paul.
Fri.—1 Timothy 1:12-17 Appointed to service.
Devotional Reading: Acts 22:1-22 Paul's defense.
Saul's Purpose

Acts 9:1-2 Saul, yet breathing out—it came from within, and out of his very nature came words and other expressions— threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord. He was opposed to Jesus Christ to the fullest extent. From the chief priest, he received written credentials, authority to arrest, bind, and bring to Jerusalem for trial any Christians found. The letters advised synagogues of Saul's authority.

Saul was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, born in Tarsus of Cilicia. He was intelligent, talented, strong in nature, and sincere in his belief. He possessed zeal, determination, and leadership. He was a thinker. An excellent education developed his natural ability to study deeply into a subject, thoroughly examining its causes and its results. The intensity of his nature required him to give entire devotion to any cause he supported. In Christ, he met his Master.
Saul's Vision

Saul the first of two surprises—that his persecution affected more than the people who suffered and struck Jesus Himself. He thought he was punishing men and women. It was a revelation to him to hear that some other Being had been struck by his blows. Persecution of saints is persecution of Jesus.
Saul's Response

Acts 9:5-7 Who art thou, Lord? He knew this was One far greater than he. He was beginning to yield. I am Jesus. Here we see the second revealed surprise to Saul—that Jesus was really God. He never got over this surprise. To the end of his days, it was the heart of the message he gave to the world— that Jesus is the Christ of God. It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks—to rebel against influences drawing toward God. This is in reference to driving oxen with a goad, sharp on the end, placed behind the rear feet to discourage the oxen to kick. To prevent the pain of injury from the pricks, the oxen must walk as the master chose. Saul was on a wrong course, and for him to rid himself of the pricks in his heart, he must obey his Master. A sinner's life rebelling against the Truth is a hard conflict.

Saul trembling and astonished—greatly surprised and touched in mind, body, and spirit—said, Lord what wilt thou have me to do? He was now completely yielded. He was acknowledging this Lord to be his Lord with the right to direct him. The Lord had a servant in Damascus whom He would use to lead Saul to the next step in his new life. The Lord said, Arise, and go into the city. He would go on to Damascus, but under different circumstances. He did not know what was next, but he was ready and obedient. Saul was not saved yet, but godly sorrow and conviction were doing their work on him. The other men of the company stood speechless— astonished also—hearing a voice, but seeing no man. They heard the voice but did not distinguish it as the voice of the Lord. We can relate to this in our worship services. When the spirit of conviction is sent in a powerful way, loud and clear, some tremble under conviction for their sins while others do not recognize it as the voice of Jesus giving invitation to a rich life in salvation.
On to Damascus

Acts 9:8-9 Saul arose . . . he saw no man: but they led him. He was blinded by the heavenly light. In Damascus, he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink —a real fast. A real burden of conviction will take away some desires, both natural appetites and unnatural ones. Real conviction causes some to stop smoking, drinking, and other things even before they are saved. They spend time in prayer because serious conviction is working on them.

Saul was a sinner, a murderer, a hater of Christ, and a persecutor of His people. What happened to Saul? Later, explaining the change in his life, he always pointed to this experience on the road as the beginning of a permanent change that lasted all of his life. There is but one explanation of such a change—the new birth. Saul was on his way to new birth—to be born of the Spirit, made alive in Christ. Saul was not yet saved, but he was on his way. He had a great start; now he must follow in obedience, step by step, the leading of God. In the next lesson, we learn of his conversion.
JUST A THOUGHT
Confession is turning the heart inside out, putting the sins out where they can be washed away.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 2
SAUL'S CONVERSION
Scripture Text: Acts 9:10-22

In the last lesson we learned: Persecution of saints is persecution of Jesus. Jesus sometimes speaks from Heaven to people on earth. A sinner's life, rebelling against the Truth, is a hard conflict. Saul yielded to God, and God led him. Hunger for God can be stronger than hunger for food.

God knows His servants. When He has a work to be done, He puts His hand upon one. He had Ananias at Damascus in the lesson today. Ananias was listening and received a blessing as well as Saul. Sometimes God looks and finds no man. When He needs you and me, will He find us faithful? Or will a work go undone, a soul unsaved, because we were not listening?
MEMORY VERSE: And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God. —Acts 9:20
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 61 Good tidings of salvation.
Tue.—Isaiah 65:1-7 A rebellious people.
Wed—Isaiah 53:1-12 Believe the Gospel.
Thu.—Romans 2:1-11 No respect of persons.
Fri.—1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 Spreading the Gospel.
Devotional Reading: Romans 10:11-21 Salvation for all.
God Instructs Ananias

Acts 9:10-14 There was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias. He was one God could use. The Lord appeared to him in a vision and told him to go into the street . . . called Straight, to the house of Judas, to Saul, of Tarsus: for behold, he prayeth. All with a desire to meet Jesus must be willing to go to Straight Street. Saul had also been given a vision. He was shown beforehand the name of the man and what he would do. Thus both Ananias and Saul were prepared for meeting. God's work is perfect. Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard by many of this man. Saul's reputation was well known among the saints. Ananias questioned the wisdom of meeting with Saul. The evil he had done to the saints at Jerusalem frightened them when they knew he had come to do the same—to bind all that call on thy name—Jesus' name.
A Chosen Vessel

Acts 9:15-16 The Lord said . . . Go thy way. Jesus knew all about Saul. He wanted Ananias to do as told. He explained, he is a chosen vessel unto me. He was to carry Jesus' name to kings, Gentiles, and Israelites. But there were great things he must suffer for the sake of Jesus' name. Christ spoke to Ananias by name. Christianity is a personal matter. God deals with us as individuals. The God who notes the fall of a sparrow knows His children by name. Sometimes we do not like the tasks to which God commissions us, yet we find later that they are the very things we would want most to do if we knew how it would end. Here Ananias was guiding into the church the most influential saint that the church has known through the centuries.

LESSON 2
Saul Becomes a Brother

Acts 9:17-18 Convinced, Ananias obeyed. The meeting was a loving, tender experience. Conviction had finished its softening work on Saul. He had counted the cost and was ready to pay the price. Ananias put his hands on Saul, calling him Brother Saul. It must have thrilled Saul's heart. Ananias came in the name of the Lord Jesus and said Jesus sent him. That was his authority. It was also the bond of love between them. The kindly greeting of Ananias and the tenderness of his touch must have convinced Saul that Christians were different from any group of people he had ever dealt with before. He came that Saul might receive . . . sight—a physical blessing—and be filled with the Holy Ghost—a spiritual blessing. Immediately the likeness of scales fell from his eyes. On the road his thinking had been changed. For three days he had been counting the cost, praying, yielding all to God, and asking for His directions. As Ananias spoke with him, his faith leaped up and took hold. His heart was open to receive Christ. Now his heart was changed also. His burden of guilt was gone. He was a new man. He arose, and was baptized. Saul did not draw back. He bore witness to all by this symbol of death to sin and new life in Christ that had been accomplished in his heart. Saul turned from misguided zeal and adhering to dead religion and following the customs of men and became an Apostle of Christ. His soul was healed. He was no longer the cruel enemy of any man; he was the loving servant of all.
Saul Bears Fruit

Acts 9:19-20 His burden of sin gone, Saul took food, he was strengthened. He stayed a time with the disciples . . . at Damascus, fellowshipping, learning, rooting in this new soil, and growing. He was not only taking in, he was giving out. Straightway—without waiting—he preached Christ . . . that he is the Son of God—the Truth he had not believed, but which now gripped his soul. He preached it in the synagogues—just where he had intended to destroy Christ's name. The letters in his pocket empowered him to punish those who called on that name. The Spirit in his heart empowered him to proclaim it. The Spirit had won his heart and made the letters useless.

Saul began to preach at once. Who licensed him? What school trained him? What church was he a member of? God had made him a member of His church, placed him, and enabled him to preach. God gave him authority and controlled him through His Spirit. Nothing more was necessary. Nothing more is necessary for anyone. Education is good, but it is not enough. Human joining and control are not good.
A Different Saul

Acts 9:21-22 All that heard him were amazed—an unbelievable change. Is not this he that destroyed ...? Yes, the same, yet no, not the same—transformed by Jesus Christ. Saul increased the more in strength—grew in grace—proving that this is the very Christ—the One anointed to be the Savior, the One God promised to send, the Son of God.
JUST A THOUGHT
No title a human being can hold carries greater honor than "Brother."

LESSON 3
PAUL BEGINS HIS MINISTRY
Scripture Text: Acts 9:23-31

Saul, later named Paul, successfully proved Jesus' deity to the Jews at Damascus. Not wanting to believe this, they were greatly angered. In Galatians 1:15-18 Paul tells us that following his conversion, he went into Arabia. He went to commune with God and meditate that he might rightly understand the Truth of the Gospel which had been revealed to him and which he was to preach. Then he returned again unto Damascus. The three years of verse 18 probably cover his stay in Arabia and his preaching in Damascus.
Paul's taking of his teaching of Christ's deity from Damascus to the Jewish synagogue brought great opposition and persecution. We reap as we sow. Barnabas was a loving Christian brother.
MEMORY VERSE: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. —2 Timothy 4:2
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Romans 8:28-39 More than conquerors.
Tue.—Ephesians 3:8-21 According to eternal purpose.
Wed.—2 Timothy 1:7-14 Called with a holy calling.
Thu.—1 Peter 1:10-23 Be holy in conduct.
Fri.—Ephesians 1:3-14 Chosen to be holy.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 24:3-14 Endure to the end.
Paul Escapes Danger

Acts 9:23-25 Paul took his teaching of Christ's deity to the point of greatest opposition, the Jewish synagogue. After many days this brought great persecution. The Jews took counsel to kill him. Determined to accomplish this end, they watched the gates day and night. Paul knew this. It must have been a frightening game of hide-and-seek until Paul's brethren took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket. As Paul quickly climbed out of the basket in the dark and started the long trip to Jerusalem (some one hundred sixty miles), he must have been thinking of times when he had been the persecutor rather than the persecuted. He was reaping what he had sowed. While he patiently reaped, he was sowing better seed for a joyous reaping that is even now continuing.
Paul at Jerusalem

Acts 9:26-28 Paul came back to Jerusalem a different man than left. He is one of the clearest examples we have of the Truth that if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17). Reaching Jerusalem, Paul assayed to join himself to the disciples—tried to fellowship with them. He was one of them now. But they were all afraid—they knew his former activity among them. They believed this to be some kind of trick, what we would call infiltration today. But Barnabas lovingly brought him to the apostles, told of his experience with the Lord and his preaching at Damascus. They were convinced. They accepted Paul, and he was with them coming in and going out—moved with them freely.

LESSON 3

Yes, Paul was a changed man. The change in him was more evident because of the public character of his wickedness and later of his preaching. Yet every redeemed soul is as much a new creature. If one is not a new being, there has been no new birth. When the sinner dies and the saint is born, the life has a new Source, new Master, new purposes and loves, and a new destiny.

We discern the character of Barnabas in the fact that when no one else had any faith in Saul's sincerity and testimony, he trusted him and went out of his way to help him. There was no man to whom Paul owed so much as he did to his loving brother, Barnabas. Since Paul was to mean so much to Christianity through the ages, the part Barnabas played in bridging the gap between Paul and the Apostles and the church was a bright jewel in his crown of Christian service.
Brethren Concerned

Acts 9:29-30 Paul, coming in and going out, spoke boldly—it took courage—in the name of the Lord Jesus. One purpose filled his life now, and by God's grace, he kept busy at it. He disputed against the Grecians—foreign Jews or proselytes brought in from outside. Paul preached boldly in spite of danger. His strong preaching of Jesus as the Son of God angered them. They, like the Damascus Jews, went about to slay him. The brethren—men of the church—found out the plan. They were more concerned than Paul for himself. They brought him . . . to Caesarea, and sent him forth to Tarsus, his home.
Rest for a Season

Acts 9:31 Then had the churches—local congregations—rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria—all of Palestine west of the Jordan River. With the chief contender out of the country, the Jew's anger cooled somewhat, and they ceased for a time to harass the church. The church could now give unhindered attention to prayer, worship, study, teaching, and service. Therefore, they were edified. They walked in the fear of the Lord—carefully obeying—and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost—the inner blessings the Holy Spirit bestowed. They were multiplied—souls were saved and added to the church. It was a time of spiritual prosperity. Their greatest strength was in the fact of the Spirit's presence in each one. They walked with sins forgiven in the comfort of the Holy Ghost. A Spirit-filled church bears spiritual fruit and wins souls.

Gospel preaching is not to be silenced because of opposition or the noisy clamor of the world. Persecution and peace can each be used of God to bless the church. We should watch for opportunities to help, encourage, and exalt a brother or sister. What can we learn here that will help us individually?
JUST A THOUGHT
As scarce as Truth is, the supply has always exceeded the demand.

LESSON 4
HEALING AND RAISING THE DEAD
Scripture Text: Acts 9:32-43
After Paul's departure for Tarsus, the Jerusalem church enjoyed a period of quiet and freedom, prospering spiritually and in numbers.

Peter went throughout all quarters contacting the saints, getting together for spiritual talk, prayer, and exhortation. This is good. It encourages, strengthens, and builds us up. Doing so, we grow in grace and knowledge and skill in God's work. Paul wrote to forsake not the assembling of ourselves together, but to exhort one another (Hebrews 10:25).

The lesson today sets forth a number of important truths. One is that God often chooses people of low estate, according to worldly standards, to fulfill some important work. Dorcas was not a person of high position. She appears to have had neither wealth nor learning. She was skilled in sewing and had a deep concern in her heart for the poor. Because of this, God used her to do a great work in His kingdom.
MEMORY VERSE: And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord. —Acts 9:42
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—James 1:1-17 Looking to God.
Tue.—2 Chronicles 7:12-22 Healing for the land.
Wed.—Psalm 41 Healing for the soul.
Thu.—Hosea 14 Healing for backsliding.
Fri.—Luke 4:16-27 Healing for the brokenhearted.
Devotional Reading: Ezekiel 37:1-14 Making dead souls live.
Aeneas Healed

Acts 9:32-35 Peter passed throughout all quarters. He went out from Jerusalem to visit the churches, probably evangelizing as he went. He came . . . to the saints . . . at Lydda. There he found Aeneas, bedfast eight years with palsy —paralysis. We would call it a hopeless case. Peter said . . . Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. He could not do this in his unhealed condition. He did not question the fact that he had not done this for eight years; he arose immediately—no hesitation. This was proof of his healing. All that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him—everyone was present and all saw the miracle— and turned to the Lord. Many souls were saved.

When God works miracles and the church acts as pleases Him, people are awakened by the nearness and power of God. They are convinced, realizing this is the God they have offended and the God they need. God does the same now as then.
The Death of Dorcas

Acts 9:36-38 There was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha in Hebrew, or Dorcas in Greek. She was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. In thinking about Dorcas, we need to give special thought to the last three words in this verse, which she did. Some people think about Christian service, dream about it, write about it, or preach about it; Dorcas performed it. She was sick, and died. They washed her and

laid her in an upper chamber. They knew what to do next. Lydda was nigh to Joppa. The disciples had heard that Peter was there. They probably had heard of Aeneas' healing. They sent . . . two men, desiring him . . . to come. In this, we see the faith of these ones at Joppa.
Dorcas Raised

Acts 9:39-41 Peter arose and went with them. Peter might have had thoughts as to why he should trouble himself with the dead when so many of the living needed his attention. But when the call came, he went without delay on what might have appeared to him a fruitless journey. On Peter's arrival, they took him to the upper chamber: and all the widows, in whose behalf Dorcas had labored so faithfully, were gathered weeping. They loved her. They showed the coats and garments which Dorcas made. Possibly they were wearing some, perhaps others were there not yet distributed. They may have asked why a good woman like this should be taken away and there be left a multitude whose passing would scarcely be missed. Peter put them all forth—to be alone with God, no dividing of attention, no unbelief to hinder, no desire for show, no long, loud praying, but simple asking. He kneeled down, and prayed—contacted God. Then turning . . . said, Tabitha, arise. Life came back in, the heart beat, and the blood flowed, the cold body warmed. She opened her eyes . . . sat up. Peter gave her his hand, and lifted her up. People who follow this pattern—solitude, silence, and prayer of faith—now as then cause mighty spiritual power to operate in their lives. He called the saints and widows—the church people and needy ones she had helped. He presented her alive. We can only imagine the glorious time they had for God's great work.

Good works are the adornment of godly women rather than jewels and costly clothing (1 Timothy 2:9-10. Dorcas wore this adornment. She was a disciple, and she was loved by the church and those she helped. She pleased God. Along with giving us the example of this godly sister, He commands us to help the poor and needy. We are to do good unto all men, especially to those of the church (Galatians 6:10). Giving should be done with no show nor boasting (Matthew 6:3-4). As we show our love for our brother, we show our love to Jesus (Matthew 25:34-40). By good works, we bring glory to the Father. This is the saint's chief desire. The Church of God, to measure to God's standard, must be full of good works.
The Effect

Acts 9:42-43 It was known throughout all Joppa. As Aeneas' healing was known, so was Dorcas' raising. Many believed in the Lord. It is not what we have that counts in God's sight or how much we give. His interest is in how we use that He has given. Let no one say that his gifts are too meager to be used in God's work. If Dorcas had a place in the Kingdom of God, you and I have a place. As her humble gifts were helpful in God's work, ours will be. But let us be sure we have the compassionate heart of Dorcas and her loving faith in Christ. Then our works will be good works as hers were.
JUST A THOUGHT
The temple of God must be richly adorned—the temple of the heart.

LESSON 5
CORNELIUS' VISION
Scripture Text: Acts 10:1-8
We have followed Peter from Lydda to Joppa on his tour visiting the saints. Today we meet a new brother and learn of an experience he had that leads Peter on to the next point.

This lesson teaches us that in the early church there was neither racial nor social intolerance. It is a good lesson on putting first the work that needs to be done for God, and second, any personal ambition one may entertain.

There is a very striking analogy between radio reception and the spiritual reception that we experience when our receiving set, the human heart, is tuned in perfectly to the Spirit and purposes of God. Peter had more than just a new message; he had a new Gospel to carry, and the Lord wanted him to carry it everywhere. God directed him.
MEMORY VERSE: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. —John 10:27
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Ephesians 2:1-13 Delivered from the world.
Tue.—Isaiah 40:25-31 The everlasting God.
Wed.—Ezekiel 36:25-33 A new heart.
Thu.—Ephesians 3:13-21 Strength for the inner man.
Fri.—John 15:9-27 Continuing in Christ's love.
Devotional Reading: Luke 19:37-44 Need to know our position.
Cornelius Prayed

Acts 10:1-2 Caesarea was the headquarters of the Roman Army in Judaea. A band was three to six hundred soldiers and was divided into six centuries of one hundred soldiers each. Each century was commanded by a centurion (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Cornelius was a centurion of . . . the Italian band, volunteers from Italy. He was a Gentile or non-Jew. He was devout to what he knew—he feared God, but had never met him personally—gave much alms to the people—probably the poor and needy. He prayed to God alway. He was in condition to hear God speak. He realized his best was not good enough.
Cornelius Sees a Vision

Acts 10:3-6 He saw in a vision . . . the ninth hour—mid-afternoon. He was fasting and praying at the time (see verse 30). He saw . . . an angel of God . . . Saying . . . Cornelius . . . he was afraid. What is it, Lord? He was ready to listen. Thy prayers and thine alms are come . . . before God. God had heard and seen. His prayer had made an impression on God at the throne of grace. God hears and answers the prayer of sinners when it concerns their salvation, the saving of their souls. This was His answer. For a memorial—a remembrance— he was in ready condition to receive something that would be stamped on the memory of both God and Cornelius.

LESSON 5

Standing out in this account of Cornelius is the fact of the rulership of the Holy Spirit. Man was not directing the actions of the individuals. No, it was the Lord, an angel of God or the Spirit Who spoke to them. It is important that we understand what state of spiritual life Cornelius was in at the time of this lesson and the next. He was devout, a just man, but he did not yet have salvation from sin. He desired something in his life that which he needed to fill the void he felt in his soul. That something was freedom from sin through salvation that only Jesus could provide.

What if Cornelius had been careless or self-willed or set on worldly thoughts? He would have missed God's voice. God was drawing him. He hungered and thirsted after righteousness, and God understood what he could not put into words. Jesus promises that such people will be filled (Matthew 5:6).

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 6
PETER'S VISION
Scripture Text: Acts 10:9-23

There was a road along the coast of Samaria that ran from Joppa to Caesarea. Last Sunday we stood at the Caesarea end of that road and looked at the vision God sent to Cornelius. Today we stand at the Joppa end and look at another vision. The visions are a pair. Together they caused two men to meet and change history. This would lead to the first Gentile being born into the church. Peter seems not to have laid out a schedule. He seems to have waited for God's direction of where to go and when.

God's plans are always in perfect order. When He told Cornelius to send for Peter, He prepared Peter to go. When He commands us, He makes the way before us. God knows the end. We can trust Him. What God commands, we can do without question. The law of clean and unclean animals is removed.
MEMORY VERSE: And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. —Acts 10:15
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Ephesians 2 Saved by grace.
Tue.—Matthew 5:38-48 Loving as God does.
Wed.—Luke 6:27-36 The actions of love.
Thu.—1 Peter 3:8-18 Returning good for evil.
Fri.—1 John 3:10-24 The love of God in us.
Devotional Reading: 1 Corinthians 12:12-26 Love each other.
The Vision of Peter

Acts 10:9-10 On the morrow—the day after Cornelius' vision and starting of men to contact Peter—as they—the men—went . . . and drew nigh to Joppa, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour—noon, dinnertime. Peter was hungry. (God wanted Peter hungry to receive the vision.) Peter fell into a trance—a state in which the soul seems carried away or absorbed in a vision.

Waiting time need not be wasted time. We are told to be redeeming the time. Parts of time some might waste in jesting, gossip, watching demoralizing TV, or pursuing wrong goals. Waiting time may be used in study, prayer, edifying talk, rest of the body, or purposeful tasks. Thus they may add up to real accomplishment for the Lord. Peter used his wait to pray. Doing so, he put himself at God's disposal and opened the door for the vision he could have missed by wrong use of his time.

Acts 10:11-13 Peter saw a vessel like a sheet caught up at the corners descending from Heaven to Earth. In it were all manner of . . . beasts . . . and creeping things, and fowls. A voice said, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat. Peter needed food. Here was food. But Peter's belief stood in the way. God's Law forbade eating unclean flesh (Leviticus 11). Some of these animals were unclean.

Why did God give this Law and later set it aside? As all of the Law, He gave it to bring mankind to Christ (Galatians 3:23-25). The Law was a type, a forerunner of something better to come. Christ was the fulfillment of it. Read Colossians 2:8-17; Romans 14:14; Hebrews 8:8-13. By the Law of clean and unclean foods, God taught people to put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean (Leviticus 10:10; Leviticus 20:25-26). Salvation in Jesus provides us a better Law. The food Law has no further use.

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 6
Call Not Thou Common

Acts 10:14-16 Peter said, Not so, Lord. Peter always quick to answer back did not realize he was contradicting God. This was a learning experience for him. God was bringing forth new Laws in a new dispensation. Now the same God Who gave the Law was giving Peter another command that took away the first. What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. If God made the unclean animals clean, they were clean. Peter was to accept them as clean. This was done thrice. The whole vision came three times to emphasize it. The lesson is true, clear, and for us all.

As the Law on food had a temporary use, so the rejection of Gentiles was temporary. It had set Israel aside for a time in preparation for Christ's coming. Now God puts no difference between any people. For the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him (Romans 10:12). As some cling to the outmoded Law of unclean foods, so some hold some people as beneath them. It is wrong to consider any class of people as common or unclean. Anyone can be saved as well as us.
What Was Its Meaning?

Acts 10:17-22 While Peter doubted in himself—wondered, meditated, pondered—what this vision . . . should mean, he felt it had greater meaning than about the animals only. Just then the men . . . from Cornelius . . . stood before the gate and inquired for Peter. While Peter thought on the vision, the Spirit said . . . men seek thee. The Spirit could talk to Peter and straighten out his thinking. Peter met the three men and was told of Cornelius' vision. The Spirit told him to go with the men, doubting nothing—without further question, sure that it was right to do so—for I have sent them. Now Peter understood the vision: Cornelius was a Gentile. Peter, a Jew, believed that the Israelite nation was chosen by God as a peculiar treasure unto Him above all people (Exodus 19:5-6). He believed salvation was for Jews only. He had believed it would be wrong to take it to the Gentiles, as they were "unclean" people, or rejected by God. Now the vision taught him that as all flesh was cleansed and fit for food, so all people were included in the offer of salvation. Christ died for ALL. Peter was to call no man common or unclean.
Peter's Obedience

Acts 10:23 God had sent the men, and Peter was glad to obey. After lodging the men overnight, Peter went away with them, accompanied by certain brethren from Joppa. What God commands, we can do without question. The Spirit never directs contrary to God's Word.
JUST A THOUGHT
Those who deserve love least need it more.

LESSON 7
SALVATION TO THE GENTILES
Scripture Text: Acts 10:24-48
We studied the visions by which God brought Cornelius and Peter together. Today we read of their meeting and its results.

Cornelius invited friends and associates to hear the message from God. Neither Peter nor any human is to be worshiped. All classes of people are to be accepted on equal terms. Peter exalted Jesus Christ. We should learn from this lesson that the sectarian walls built between saints are wrong. What God accepts, we should accept.

How deep is the experience of one who is not concerned for the salvation of those near him? When God has control of a heart, He reaches out from that heart to others. God is love. Concern for others is necessary if we are to win them to Christ.
MEMORY VERSE: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. —Acts 10:35
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—John 14:25-31 The Spirit will teach.
Tue.—John 16:5-15 The Spirit must be sent.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 2:6-16 Natural man cannot receive it.
Thu.—Romans 8:8-17 The Spirit is life.
Fri.—Jude 1:10-23 These have not the Spirit.
Devotional Reading: John 15:18-27 World hates the Spirit.
Cornelius and Peter Meet

Acts 10:24-27 On the morrow . . . they entered into Caesarea—about thirty miles from Joppa. Cornelius waited for them. What anticipation he must have felt, wondering what was in store for them. He called together his kinsmen and near friends. His faith looked for reward. He knew God was sending rich spiritual help. In concern that others share it, he filled his house. Cornelius met him. He could not wait, but went to meet Peter. He associated Peter with the angel and God's message, and he felt Peter was superhuman. He fell down ... and worshipped him. He did not understand; he was ignorant of the wrong he did. See Matthew 4:10. Peter corrected him immediately—took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man—the same as you. No man is to be worshipped. They went in, talking as they went, and found many waiting to hear.

The Bible shows Peter as a very fallible man. To set him or any other man or woman in a position of exalted power and honor is wrong. It is usurping Christ's place. Christ is the Head of the church. He said, Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren (Matthew 23:8). Peter never assumed a position other than a brother in the church, exercising the spiritual gifts God gave him.
Peter Begins

Acts 10:28-33 Ye know . . . it is . . . unlawful . . . for a . . . Jew to . . . come unto one of another nation. (See Deuteronomy 7:1-6.) Then why did Peter come? God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. He changed his position at God's Word. He accepted these people. Peter asked why they had sent for him. He was ready to serve. A question is often a good starting point. Cornelius recounted his vision. Here we see the power of prayer and fasting. We are all here present before God—they came before

God, not Peter only—to hear all things that are commanded thee of God. It was God's message they wanted, not the message bearer. They were expecting to receive from God.
God Is No Respecter of Persons

Acts 10:34-35 Peter . . . said . . . God is no respecter of persons. Here it is, the Truth about human relationship in this new Gospel dispensation, brought forth by Christ making salvation possible to all mankind. What a revolutionary doctrine! Peter may have spoken with considerable calmness, but it must have caused some soul-searching in his own heart to say that God has no favorites, does not look to see who is asking before bestowing a blessing. In every nation—no race is shut out—he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. Here we see both faith and works united as conditions of acceptance with God. Neither alone is enough. Our trust must all be in Jesus. Nothing we can do will save us. Our deeds must be righteous. We must live holy lives (1 Peter 1:15-16).
Peter's Sermon

Acts 10:36-43 Peter exalted Jesus Christ. He told them that Christ was the Word of God, the Lord of all, bringing peace to man. He told of Jesus' death, burial, and resurrection. Peter said he knew all this because they saw it with their own eyes. Us, who did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead. As he talked, the people opened their hearts to all that God had for them.
God Blesses the Gentiles

Acts 10:44-48 While Peter yet spake—uttered the words remission of sins—very quickly the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word. All that heard believed. The Joppa brethren were astonished to see Gentiles receive salvation. It was a sight so marvelous to behold that Peter and his companions could scarcely believe their eyes. They magnified God, as those in Jerusalem when first the Spirit came (Acts 2:4-11). Can any man forbid water to baptize these? They had the spiritual reality inside, now were ready to testify to it by the outward symbol.
We learn from this that baptism does not save from sin. They asked Peter to tarry certain days. They desired his fellowship and teaching. They had found a new love, the love of Christ.

We should learn from this vision that sectarian walls built between saints are wrong. If a man is saved and Christ dwells within his heart, it means God has accepted him. He may hold some false teachings which prohibit his being placed as a leader, but he should be treated as a brother. Whom God accepts, we should accept.
JUST A THOUGHT
Faith keeps the man who keeps the faith.

LESSON 8
PETER'S RESPONSE TO HIS BRETHREN
Scripture Text: Acts 11:1-18

Sometimes one has not only to carry out a project, but also to defend his action before those who question it. Such was Peter's experience after he went to Cornelius. Sometimes when our action is questioned by our brethren, we are tempted to be resentful and belligerent. It is better to assume that the critics are also desirous of doing God's will and keeping the church clean.

Those in the lesson today were. Peter kindly but frankly explained. Very recently he had held the same attitude as these brethren now held. He treated them with the same understanding God had used in teaching him. Let us look at the result as recorded in this lesson.
MEMORY VERSE: Forasmuch then as God gave them the like gift as he did unto us, who believed on the Lord Jesus Christ; what was I, that I could withstand God? —Acts 11:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Galatians 3:6-18 The example of Abraham.
Tue.—Galatians 2:11-21 Paul's opposition to Peter.
Wed.—1 Timothy 5:17-25 Rebuke before all.
Thu.—Matthew 9:9-17 Jesus came to sinners.
Fri.—Romans 1:8-17 Greeks included.
Devotional Reading: Luke 2:25-35 A light to Gentiles also.
The Criticism

Acts 11:1-3 The apostles and brethren . . . heard . . . Gentiles had . . . received the word. They were Spirit-filled men, yet their ignorance or mistaken belief led them to oppose the salvation of Gentiles. They that were of the circumcision—Jews—contended with Peter. Notice, they held their peace until they met with Peter face-to-face. They did not hash it over and form opinions against Peter on what they heard. The church needs to learn this lesson today. Their criticism was, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised. Gentiles were unclean to the Israelites; they were people outside of the favor of God. Didst eat with them—worse. Eating together signified friendship, equality. Peter's action seemed to his brethren to be a lowering of God's standard. They felt he had been disrespectful to God's calling. Peter admitted their charges as true. They wanted the facts from Peter himself. Peter did not resent their honest criticism.
Peter's Explanation

Acts 11:4-11 Peter rehearsed the matter . . . expounded it by order—told it all plainly and explained it step-by-step. He respected the honesty of their position and with love showed the facts that they might come to an understanding of the Truth. Peter told of his vision. His explanation was not in self-defense, but in defense of God's Word. The middle wall of partition was now pulled down. The Jews and Gentiles are called to become one flock, under one Shepherd and Bishop of souls. Peter had not opened the door; God did.

LESSON 8
Points in Peter's Defense

Acts 11:12-17 The Spirit bade me go. (1) Peter's action was not of his own planning. It was obedience to God's Spirit. These brethren had the Spirit and understood Peter. These six brethren accompanied me. (2) He had witnesses. They witnessed the happening, agreed with no objection. (3) Peter briefly told of Cornelius' vision, which agreed with his own. Call for Simon—Peter—who shall tell thee words whereby thou . . . shall be saved. Forasmuch then—since—God gave them the like gift—the Holy Spirit, as he did to us. (4) They had obtained the gift the same way. They believed on the Lord Jesus Christ; what was I, that I could withstand God? (5) Peter pointed out his lack of authority in this. The act was God's, not his. Only God can send the Holy Spirit. (6) Peter plead his responsibility to God. Since God is perfect and all-powerful, Peter had no right to question His acts, only to cooperate with Him. God, Who made, at first, the distinction between Jews and Gentiles, has a right to remove it, whenever and by whatever means He pleases. Peter saw both Jews and Gentiles going to Heaven.
The Apostles' Conclusion

Acts 11:18 These brethren were servants of God; they were Apostles. Peter, a short time ago, had felt and believed as they. They did not have the authority to decide this among themselves. It did not rest in them to make rules and creeds and doctrines, to legislate for the church. They were not a governing body. That authority is God's alone. They were only servants to carry out the commands of Christ as the Spirit directed. When they heard these things, they held their peace—had nothing to say. blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 9
THE CHURCH SCATTERED BY PERSECUTION
Scripture Text: Acts 11:19-30

The persecution of the brethren following the death of Stephen scattered the saints far and wide, and so, instead of extinguishing the fire of the new faith, succeeded only in spreading it. Now they were conscious that the Gospel was meant for all men everywhere. Now all nations could receive the Christian faith. Here we notice that God does great things through plain, ordinary, humble people. We observe, also, that evangelism sometimes begins not in public meeting but in private conversation.

There were many Spirit-given gifts in the Jerusalem church. Using them under the direction of the Spirit gave this church leadership, administered in love and brotherhood, not in dominion and authority. Today we get a look at the scattering of these saints and the result of their witness.
MEMORY VERSE: And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord. —Acts 11:21
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Matthew 6:1-18 God will reward openly.
Tue.—Proverbs 10:11-22 Love covers all sin.
Wed.—3 John 1-12 Walk in the Truth.
Thu.—2 John 4-11 Follow God's Commandments.
Fri.—Colossians 3:1-17 The center of Christian life.
Devotional Reading: 1 Corinthians 10:23-33 Glorify God.
Many People Believed

Acts 11:19-21 They which were scattered . . . travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch. Fleeing for their lives, the urge of the Spirit within was so strong that they went preaching the word. Some preached unto the Jews only. Some . . . were men of Cyprus and Cyrene. They preached Christ to the Greeks. Their preaching was successful because the hand of the Lord was with them. This again shows that it is God's will that the Gospel be taken to Gentiles. A great number believed, and turned unto the Lord.

We read this often as we go through the Acts. Salvation work is a continual thing, not occasional, the usual, not extraordinary. We should not be satisfied to see a few saved now and then during the year. We want to see more. In Acts, we see God's normal way. This is what He will do for us if we yield to Him as these people did. Obey Him. Expect continual salvation work. Antioch was a tough place in which to found a Christian congregation. It was a place for nice people and timid people to stay away from. There was much sin there, so much that even the Romans spoke with disdain of the city's moral life. Yet it was to this wicked city that the saints who fled Jerusalem after Stephen's death brought the Gospel. And it was to the Gentiles, who the Jews believed to be beyond the boundaries of God's mercy, that these saints preached the Gospel.

LESSON 9
Barnabas Sent to Investigate

Acts 11:22-24 The church in Jerusalem, hearing of the evangelization of Greeks, sent Barnabas. He was also from Cyprus (4:36). He was to go as far as Antioch. In Antioch Barnabas saw the grace of God—it was God's work, these people had the real goods. He was glad. No objection from him. He rejoiced in the Truth. He exhorted them to cleave unto the Lord—to continue holding fast to Jesus. They should do it with purpose of heart—determination, from the heart pressing on to the goal set before them. Barnabas was a good man. Barnabas partook of this quality of God because God was in him. He was full of the Holy Ghost and of faith. While he was in Antioch, much people was added unto the Lord—were saved.

The Jerusalem church seems to have exercised leadership in the activities. This does not mean it held superior rights of authority or was a governing body. We see brotherly concern, investigation and advice, but no rulership. The rulership of the Holy Spirit is very evident as we move through our study. The Apostles had associated with Jesus in Jerusalem; they had greater experience than most others had. Since the Holy Spirit came first in Jerusalem, they had more time to become established. The Apostles at Jerusalem, as human instruments, had been given the Spirit's gifts and knew how to use them. If we are faithful where we happen to be and wait patiently upon the Lord, He will move us into greater areas of service when we are ready for them.
Barnabas Brings Paul

Acts 11:25-26 Then Barnabas went to Tarsus for to seek Saul. When he had found him—It is apparent that he had to look for him, remembering that Tarsus was Paul's home, where they had sent him for safety (Acts 9:30). Now the loving heart of Barnabas wanted Paul to enjoy these good meetings at Antioch and the newly saved to benefit from Paul's clear teaching. He brought him unto Antioch, where for a year they both taught much people. The disciples were called Christians first in Antioch—like Christ, followers of Christ. People must have seen a resemblance strong enough to warrant the name. Do they see that resemblance in us?

Barnabas did not forget Paul. He had brought Paul to the church at first (Acts 9:27). His action then in bringing Paul into fellowship with the church there, and now bringing him back into active duty, may be the connecting link which gave the world the great service of the Apostle Paul.

Let us take this opportunity to stir up our minds in way of remembrance of what it means to be a follower of Christ. It means, first of all, to follow Christ in His teachings. These teachings are contrary to the teachings of the world. Once we have decided to be followers of Christ, we have to bid goodbye to the world's ways and walk the road Christ walked. This He teaches through His Word. Read and study it. The Bible is the Christian's road map.
Antioch Christians Believed the Prophets

Acts 11:27-30 Came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch. Prophets deliver to the people whatever message God gives them. One, Agabus, was given forecasts of the future. (Acts 21:10-11). He told them by the Spirit—not his own judgment— that great dearth—scarcity, want, lack of food on account of crop failure— was coming throughout all the world. The Antioch disciples believed the message. They determined to send relief to the church in Judaea. Each gave voluntarily and according to his ability. This is God's way. They chose Barnabas and Saul to carry the offering to Jerusalem to the elders for distribution.
JUST A THOUGHT

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 10
AN ANGEL IN PRISON
Scripture Text: Acts 12:1-19
In our last lesson we learned of a famine in Judaea. The church in Antioch sent money and food to the church in Jerusalem, and Paul and Barnabas were selected to take it.

About this time Herod began a new persecution of the church and killed James, the brother of John. Seeing it pleased the Jews, he put Peter in prison, but the church prayed for him continually. The night before Herod was to bring him forth for trial, the angel of the Lord appeared in the prison and caused the chains to fall off Peter's ankles and led Peter out of the prison and set him free. Peter went to the home of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where the church was gathered praying.

In our lesson today we learn that we should spread the Gospel of Christ in spite of persecution. We should pray, expecting God to answer, even to bring miracles. We must not question God's wisdom and judgment. The thing of greatest importance is that God's program goes forward.
MEMORY VERSE: Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh: is there anything too hard for me? —Jeremiah 32:27
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—2 Corinthians 4:7-18 A tried life.
Tue.—Matthew 5:10-20 Light of the world.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 5:1-15 A confident ministry.
Thu.—Luke 21:8-19 Things must come to pass.
Fri.—Ephesians 6:10-20 Put on whole armor of God.
Devotional Reading: 1 Peter 1:3-12 Kept by power of God.
Persecution by Herod

Acts 12:1-3 About that time—when Barnabas and Saul brought the relief gifts from Antioch to Jerusalem—Herod began to vex certain of the church. The church had enjoyed a period of rest from persecution, but it did not last. Herod Agrippa I was king of Judaea, Samaria, and other parts. He was a strict observer of the law, and he sought with success the favor of the Jews. With this in mind, he put James to death. The church was making great progress throughout the land. Opposition brought persecution. Seeing the death of James pleased the Jews, Herod put Peter in prison.

Why did God allow James to be killed, yet saved Peter? This is not ours to question. Jesus had told His people these things would be brought to pass (Luke 21:16-17). Death cannot destroy what has been put in God's hands. No persecution or death can destroy our life in Christ.
Peter's Imprisonment

Acts 12:4-6 Herod kept Peter secure, he thought. He was inside prison walls, guarded by sixteen soldiers, bound with two chains. Herod intended after Easter to bring him forth to the people—the Jews. The mind of the people would no doubt have been to kill Peter. They bitterly hated Jesus Whom Peter preached. But

prayer was made . . . of the church . . . for him. On the last night before Herod would have brought him forth to meet the mob, Peter, bound and guarded, slept between two soldiers.

God gives us this record to show what He will also do for us. The church prayed without ceasing unto God. All trust was in Him, not in their own works. God answered just in time, not before. God is never late.

Acts 12:7-10 The angel of the Lord came . . . a light shined . . . he smote Peter . . . Arise . . . his chains fell off. Peter obeyed, dressed, and followed, thinking he was seeing a vision. Past one ward, two wards, through the city gate which opened . . . of his own accord . . . through one street, and the angel departed. The soldiers remained ignorant and helpless. Truly, with God all things are possible.
Peter Knew Where to Go

Acts 12:11-17 Left alone, Peter knew this was real, that he was not dreaming. I know . . . the Lord . . . hath delivered me. All the praise belonged to God. Peter considered—it was night. Who would be awake to receive him? Where would he find the saints? He went to the house of Mary, sister of Barnabas and mother of John Mark. The saints gathered there often. Many were gathered . . . praying. These prayers were the reason for Peter's release. Peter knocked. Rhoda was so surprised that she failed to open the door, but ran to tell. The surprise was so great that the others did not believe her at first. Thou art mad—insane. Then, as Rhoda insisted it was Peter, they said, It is his angel, or he is dead, and this is his ghost. Those saints were like we are. They had to overcome the same thoughts we have to overcome. Opening the door and seeing Peter, they were astonished. Had they no faith as they prayed? They did, for their prayers were answered. But this miracle was a greater answer than they expected. Perhaps they thought Herod would give lenient judgment. But God does better than we can ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). Peter quieted the people, and then told his wonderful story, how the Lord had brought him out. Leaving these saints, Peter went into another place, probably to escape re-arrest.

Mary was an active saint of the Jerusalem church. We have observed the Christian character of her brother Barnabas. John Mark, her son, was an evangelist with Barnabas and Paul (Acts 12:25; 2 Timothy 4:11). Her home was a gathering place for prayer. We need more homes like this.
Herod's Reaction

Acts 12:18-19 When day arrived, there was no small stir among the soldiers. It meant life or death to them, yet they were ignorant of the happenings. To let a prisoner escape was a capital crime. After examination, Herod commanded that they should be put to death. Unjust? Yes, but Herod did not know God nor what He had done.

Sixteen soldiers suffered death unjustly. This is part of God's plan in both the Old Testament and the New. God's program has often brought death or suffering to some, as the slaughter of babies at Jesus' coming (Matthew 2:16), the death of people and animals in the Flood (Genesis 7:21-22), and the loss of swine at the healing of the demon-possessed man (Mark 5:11-13). Why? Because of the influence of sin. God's program is not inferior, that it should wait on the convenience of every cause. It must be carried on. He will not allow any power to stand in His way of progress. It is not ours to question His judgment. Tragedies occur because it is a sinful world, not because God desires them. God's program will go forward. Can He use you?
JUST A THOUGHT
If you don't want the fruits of sin, stay out of the orchard.

LESSON 11
HEROD'S DESTRUCTION
Scripture Texts: Acts 12:19-25; Proverbs 6:16-17
Herod, King of Judaea, Samaria, and other dominions of Rome, had been persecuting the church at Jerusalem. He had killed James and imprisoned Peter. God miraculously rescued Peter.

How much we sometimes pay for worthless trifles in this life. In our lesson we are told of people who gave honor to Herod, but it was only lip service offered to gain favor for them. It was empty flattery. It was wrong. Yet for receiving this blasphemous praise of the people, he paid his soul. We see the result of pride in the heart of man.
MEMORY VERSE: Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name. —1 Chronicles 16:29a
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Galatians 6:1-10 Self-deception.
Tue.—Romans 12:1-10 Careful of conduct.
Wed.—Proverbs 21:1-12 Treasure of the wicked.
Thu.—Proverbs 22:1-16 The value of a good name.
Fri.—Psalm 40:1-10 No respect for the proud.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 23:1-12 The humble exalted.
Seeking Herod's Favor

Acts 12:19-20 Not finding his prisoner, Peter, Herod ordered the keepers executed. Then, leaving bereaved hearts behind him, he went down to Caesarea, where was his official residence. Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon, cities farther north along the coast. They came to him from there, used the clever strategy of first making friends with Blastus, Herod's chamberlain, then worked up to desire peace with the king himself. This was not because they admired Herod or desired his personal friendship. It was because their country was nourished by the king's country. It was for their own selfish advantage, for their economic welfare. As saints, we must never join hands with the world for any personal benefit or gain.
Herod's Oration

Acts 12:21-22 Upon a set day—arranged and announced—Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne—with all the power of state and much pomp and show—made an oration—an elaborate public discourse treating an important subject in a formal and dignified manner. The people gave a shout—applause. The praise was personal and the very highest. It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. It was not sincere, it was flattery, designed to win Herod's favor for themselves. It was blasphemy. It was wrong for them to give and wrong for Herod to accept. Raising any person or thing to the place of God is idolatry. It is wrong to take glory to ourselves. All glory belongs to God, but Herod took it to himself. To speak words of thanks and appreciation to our brethren for a good work is not giving them God's glory. This is part of the debt of love we owe them.

Here is a man, a strict keeper of the Law ceremonies, raised to political power and honor, bound by sin, trying to rise on false glory to a place of godliness. He was building on a false foundation which would not hold, and he fell. His house was built on the sand. When it fell, as all such must, great was the fall of it. Read Galatians 6:3. Look not with scorn. Look not with self-righteousness, thinking it could not happen to you.

LESSON 11
Herod's Punishment

Acts 12:23 Immediately—usually the bulk of sin's punishment is deferred, but it is always certain, unless forgiven. The angel of the Lord smote him. Angels are God's servants, sent sometimes to bless, sometimes to punish. God punished Herod's sin at once. Why? Because he gave not God the glory. He accepted the blasphemous praise of the people. He took it as being due him. He did not refuse it and pass it on to God. He gave up the ghost—destroyed physically and spiritually. He paid with his soul.

We are not kings. Most of us do not make orations to a nation. But there is a danger facing all of us. Herod's trouble did not start in what he did. It lay deeper. He had much pride and self-righteousness and arrogance in his heart. The capacity for pride seems overgrown in human nature. It lies in every unregenerate heart (Mark 7:21-23). It is easily revived by success or praise. To see the ever-threatening danger, look at the number of sad wrecks it is causing. Often a talented, promising one lets success "go to his head" and falls from usefulness, a victim to pride. We can be proud of something or proud of nothing, proud of our pride or proud of our humility. Whatever the form, it is still pride. Pride in the heart is sin (Proverbs 21:4).
The Sin of Pride

Proverbs 6:16-17 These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: A proud look . . . (See also Proverbs 8:13.) Pride is selfish. It is desire for glory. It is an overvaluation of the esteem of one's self. It is a lust of the flesh, and is not of the Father (1 John 2:16). All glory and honor belong to God (Psalm 115:1). To take any upon ourselves is stealing from Him. All the good that we have comes from Him.
The Remedy for Pride

Jesus' warning to watch needs to be diligently obeyed in the area of pride. Many saved ones have been lost over this temptation, blindly going on thinking themselves rich, when really they are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17-18). This need not be. Jesus stands ready to save to the uttermost. He asks us to buy of Him gold tried in the fire, real, spiritual riches. He will lift you out of the mire of sin to His plane of salvation. He will cleanse the heart of pride, arrogance, and every defilement. Jesus Christ is the only remedy.
Success of the Gospel Continued

Acts 12:24-25 But the word of God grew and multiplied. This is not a change of subject. The conjunction but connects it with what went before, connects it in contrast. Herod had set out to destroy the Gospel by killing its promoters. He has gone down in defeat, while the Gospel lives and grows. Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem to Antioch, when they had fulfilled their ministry of delivering the gift from the Antioch church to the church in Judaea. They took with them John Mark as they continued the spread of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Fighting against the power of the Gospel is a losing battle.
JUST A THOUGHT
Never forget that the way up is down.

LESSON 12
THE GOSPEL MEETS OPPOSITION
Scripture Text: Acts 13:1-13

The Antioch church was a healthy, living church. Souls were being saved. Saints were being given spiritual gifts and placed in God's work. In a normal church this is a continuing process. At present there is a great lack of workers. Churches are in great need of pastors. Sunday schools are in need of teachers. Everywhere is work to be done, souls to reach. God will have workers if we put ourselves at His disposal. Consecrate, prepare, pray, expect His call and answer it.

The spiritual gifts of Barnabas and Paul caused them to be chosen. The Holy Spirit did the choosing. The Holy Spirit spoke through prayer. Fasting and prayer were practiced. The Holy Spirit in Paul gave him power against false prophecy and sorcery—a work of the devil. It was God, not Paul, who punished this enemy of the Gospel.
MEMORY VERSE: As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. —Acts 13:2
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—1 Corinthians 12:1-14 Different gifts, same Spirit.
Tue.—1 Corinthians 15:1-20 A secure ministry.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 4 A tried ministry.
Thu.—2 Corinthians 3:1-14 A ministry of glory.
Fri.—Philippians 1:3-17 Defend the Gospel.
Devotional Reading: Ephesians 1:3-14 A Gospel of salvation.
The Holy Spirit Speaks

Acts 13:1-2 Prophets and teachers were in the Antioch church. The Holy Spirit had given the gifts of prophecy and teaching to individuals from various places and backgrounds. Now all were one in Christ. Because of the fact that people met in homes and, therefore, in small groups, a larger number of teachers and prophets were necessary. As they ministered to the Lord—served Him in prayer and worship—and fasted—did not eat—the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul. They were to be set apart for His work. It is a risky thing to yield ourselves to the Holy Spirit, unless we are prepared to take orders.
Obedience to the Spirit

Acts 13:3-5 First, the church fasted and prayed again, this time for one specific purpose. They laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul—sanctioning God's action and asking Him to enable them for the work. Barnabas and Saul went as the Spirit led; the brethren did not send them. Their journey took them to Seleucia, Cyprus, and Salamis. They preached in the synagogues. Their preaching was to Jews and Gentiles both. They had . . . John to their minister—to help them, to serve. Paul did not rule the church. He was sent by the Holy Spirit. The Antioch church did not rule; they were told by the Holy Spirit what to do. If we search the Bible through, we cannot find any ruler of the church but the Holy Spirit.

LESSON 12
The Devil Opposes Truth

Acts 13:6-8 At Paphos was a sorcerer and false prophet named Elymas. He was with a man of high position. This man, Sergius Paulus, was sincere and enough interested to ask to hear the word of God. To hinder Sergius Paulus from hearing the Gospel and becoming a servant of God, the devil led his servant Elymas to withstand Barnabas and Saul. He tried to turn away the deputy from the faith. What a terrible thing to do!

God has set His face against those who work magic and sorcery (Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6). Sorcery is still here. It often goes by the name of Christian and calls itself a church, but always it is opposed to God and His Truth. It claims to heal and tell fortunes and reveal secret wisdom by the power of God's Spirit, but really works by the spirits of devils. Sorcery or spiritism is dangerous. Revelation 21:8 tells the end of sorcerers. Elymas was a false prophet, one who claimed to have a divine commission to speak in God's name. But God says of such that they have a deceitful heart (Jeremiah 14:14). Religious teachers not in contact with God and who pervert the Bible are false prophets. They are among us yet today. Judgment and damnation is their lot (2 Peter 2:1-3).
Elymas Punished

Acts 13:9-11 Then Saul (or Paul) . . . filled with the Holy Ghost steps forward. He does not wait for Barnabas. The Spirit speaking through Paul rebuked Elymas severely. He called Elymas full of all subtlety and all mischief—sly and evil motives—child of the devil—not God's—enemy of all righteousness—destroying the very thing he needed most. This is the tragic but true story of our day. The hand of the Lord is upon thee— It was the Lord's act, not that of Paul. Thou shalt be blind . . . for a season. His blindness was to be total. He could not even see the sun in its brightness; but it was not to be perpetual, it was only for a time that God deemed sufficient. It would be long enough to prevent his opposition to the Gospel. And immediately Elymas was blind. When he became blind, his manner changed. No longer did he try to lead the deputy away from the Truth, but rather sought someone to lead him along the way.

Paul here steps forward as a leader. He has new sureness and strength. The Holy Spirit fitted him for his work. From now on, we read his name first—Paul and Barnabas. Paul's strong nature shows through here. He spoke severely. Another might have spoken as truly but not so firm. He was to meet a cruel world and many enemies of Christ. God could use his nature in the place He put him. The power of the Holy Spirit that Jesus promised made prophets and teachers. It gave Paul discernment to understand the character of Elymas and to pronounce blindness upon him, and to teach and win the deputy.
The Deputy Believes

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 13
PROGRESS IN GOD'S KINGDOM
Scripture Text: Acts 13:14-52

Paul and Barnabas were on their first missionary journey. They came to the city of Antioch, and on the Sabbath Day, they went into the synagogue and sat down. After reading a portion of the Old Testament, the ruler of the synagogue called upon them to speak. Paul began with a brief history of Israel from the time they were in bondage in Egypt until David ruled over the land of Palestine. Then he showed that John the Baptist was the forerunner of Christ and that Christ fulfilled the prophecies of the Old Testament. He reminded the Jews of how they had crucified Christ, but that God had raised Him from the dead and that all people could be saved by believing in Him. When the Jews had left the building, the Gentiles asked that Paul preach these same things to them on the next Sabbath. When the Jews saw the multitudes that came to hear Paul, they were jealous and rose up against them and drove them out of the region.
MEMORY VERSE: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. —Luke 24:47
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Romans 3:9-25— All have sinned and need Christ.
Tue.— Romans 1:18-32 —Turning from God to sin.
Wed.—1 John 5:1-13 — Salvation is in Christ.
Thu.—Hebrews 9:21-28 — Christ the perfect sacrifice.
Fri.—Isaiah 40:12-31 God gives power to man.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 24:3-14— Enduring unto the end.
An Invitation to Speak

Acts 13:14-22 Paul and Barnabas went into the synagogue on the Sabbath because they knew there were people worshiping there. They sat down. They made themselves available for God's use there. The rulers of the synagogue called upon them to speak, if you have any word of exhortation. Paul began with a brief history of Israel with which these people were familiar—from the time they were in bondage in Egypt until David reigned over the land.
He Preached Jesus

Acts 13:23-37 Of this man's [David's] seed hath God . . . raised . . . a Savior, Jesus. This was the heart of his message. According to his [God's] promise—fulfilling prophecy. Paul showed that John the Baptist was the forerunner of Christ and that Christ fulfilled the prophecies of the Old Testament. John the Baptist also predicted Christ's coming. The promise came first to the Jews. And we declare unto you glad tidings . . . the promise ... God hath fulfilled . . . in that he hath raised up Jesus again—the Resurrection.

The Jerusalem Jews heard the Prophets (Old Testament Books) read every Sabbath (Acts 13:27). Yet they did not know them. When He came, they did not recognize the Christ the Prophets told about. To escape the same tragedy, we need to read and understand the Bible while we have the opportunity. Our children need to be taught the Bible. We will be judged by it and need to know what it says. Pray the Lord to open His Word to you.

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 13
Jesus Alone Justifies

Acts 13:38-41 Through this man [Jesus] is preached . . . forgiveness of sins. All sinful humans need forgiveness more than anything else. It is only in Christ. By him [Christ] all that believe—who by faith take Him and His promise—are justified—cleared of guilt—from all things—all sins, saved to the uttermost. Justification cannot be obtained by the law of Moses. Paul had placed two methods of salvation opposite each other. He said one was perfectly successful, the other a perfect failure. The method he called successful was fiercely opposed by the Jews. The one he called a failure was that held by them. He warned them of the danger of rejecting Christ, quoting Habakkuk 1:5 (verse 41). Their unbelief was prophesied long before.

Acts 13:42-43 There were many Gentiles in the audience who, because they believed in one God, had accepted the Jewish faith. Many of the Gentiles remained after the meeting and asked for this preaching again the next Sabbath. A good number of Jews and proselytes believed. They followed Paul and Barnabas, hungry for spiritual food. The Apostles encouraged them to continue in the grace of God. The Apostles' advice to them needs to be repeated over and over. Only those who endure unto the end will be finally saved (Matthew 24:13). To endure, we must have grace. Grace is a supply of God's own life which He pours into the lives of His children as we need it. To obtain it, stay in contact with God. Live in His strength, not yours.

The Jews followed the Law. Now the Law was fulfilled in Christ, but the Jews would not believe. They held back for the old forms and symbols. These could never save them. If we think we can be justified by our obedience to forms, by going to church, by baptism, by signing a card, by good works, etc., we are like the Jews. We can be justified only by believing in Christ.
Opposition From the Jews

Acts 13:44-52 The next Sabbath day came almost the whole city—many gathered which excited envy in the Jews. It widened the gap between them and the Gentiles. They opposed Paul's teaching, contradicting and blaspheming. Paul boldly told them that the word of God was to be spoken to them first. He told them if they rejected God's Word and everlasting life, we turn to the Gentiles. He recalled God's Words to him sending him to the Gentiles and to take salvation unto the ends of the earth (Acts 9:15; Acts 22:15, Acts 22:21; Acts 26:16-18). Gentiles believed and spread the Word to the ends of the earth. The Jews raised persecution and drove out the Apostles, who left filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost. Acts 9:16 was beginning to be fulfilled in Paul.

Paul saw issues clearly. He wanted others to. God, not men, taught Paul the Gospel (Galatians 1:11-12). He presented it boldly to the very ones who would oppose it most. Many would fear to do so. Paul used no shallow talk of all going to the same place, or all being children of God. He knew the deadly disease these people suffered from. He knew the remedy that saved him. He knew from his experience that it would work. He laid it plainly before the people. When they refused it, he was through with them because God was through with them. They had judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life. By their words and conduct, they had passed sentence upon themselves and, in effect, had stated that they were unworthy of the grace of the Gospel. The Gospel was to them a savor of death unto death.
JUST A THOUGHT
A method of finding work to do is to make ourselves available to God and wait for an opening and His leading.

Paul used no shallow talk of all going to the same place, or all being children of God.
He knew the deadly disease these people suffered from.
He knew the remedy that saved him.
He knew from his experience that it would work.
He laid it plainly before the people.
When they refused it, he was through with them because God was through with them.
They had judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life.
By their words and conduct, they had passed sentence upon themselves and, in effect, had stated that they were unworthy of the grace of the Gospel.
The Gospel was to them a savor of death unto death.

lines.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
THE POWER OF HOLY GHOST
CONVICTION
Scripture Text: Acts 9:1-9
Last week we studied of the salvation of one individual— the
eunuch from Africa. God used a man to reach him, and it seemed
such an easy task. Today we study another individual in his move to
Christ. God used a miraculous vision from Heaven and physical
means to reach Saul of Tarsus, or Paul. This seemed a more difficult
task.
This quarter we go on with our study of the early church as told
in Acts. The evidence found here of the power of God to change
lives and use those lives to His glory should move us to seek that
same power. God gave us this history to excite like action. He put
this picture before us to show how He will use us also. No one can
do this in his own strength. We must do it as these saints of Acts did
it—by the power of the Holy Spirit, under His direction.
MEMORY VERSE: And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord
said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.
—Acts 9:6
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Acts 26:1-20 Paul's testimony.
Tue.—Philippians 2:1-16 Giving up all for Christ.
Wed.—Galatians 1:11-17 Paul's authority of divine origin.
Thu.—1 Timothy 1:1-11 Glorious Gospel committed to Paul.
Fri.—1 Timothy 1:12-17 Appointed to service.
Devotional Reading: Acts 22:1-22 Paul's defense.
Saul's Purpose
Acts 9:1-2 Saul, yet breathing out—it came from within, and out of his very nature came words and other
expressions— threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord. He was opposed to Jesus Christ
to the fullest extent. From the chief priest, he received written credentials, authority to arrest, bind, and bring to
Jerusalem for trial any Christians found. The letters advised synagogues of Saul's authority.
Saul was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, born in Tarsus of Cilicia. He was intelligent, talented, strong in
nature, and sincere in his belief. He possessed zeal, determination, and leadership. He was a thinker. An
excellent education developed his natural ability to study deeply into a subject, thoroughly examining its causes
and its results. The intensity of his nature required him to give entire devotion to any cause he supported. In
Christ, he met his Master.
Saul's Vision
Acts 9:3-4 As he journeyed . . . near Damascus . . . a light from heaven shone. Saul fell to the earth. He
had met a Power greater than his. A voice said, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? Here was revealed to

Saul the first of two surprises—that his persecution affected more than the people who suffered and struck Jesus
Himself. He thought he was punishing men and women. It was a revelation to him to hear that some other Being
had been struck by his blows. Persecution of saints is persecution of Jesus.
Saul's Response
Acts 9:5-7 Who art thou, Lord? He knew this was One far greater than he. He was beginning to yield. I
am Jesus. Here we see the second revealed surprise to Saul—that Jesus was really God. He never got over this
surprise. To the end of his days, it was the heart of the message he gave to the world— that Jesus is the Christ of
God. It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks—to rebel against influences drawing toward God. This is in
reference to driving oxen with a goad, sharp on the end, placed behind the rear feet to discourage the oxen to
kick. To prevent the pain of injury from the pricks, the oxen must walk as the master chose. Saul was on a
wrong course, and for him to rid himself of the pricks in his heart, he must obey his Master. A sinner's life
rebelling against the Truth is a hard conflict.
Saul trembling and astonished—greatly surprised and touched in mind, body, and spirit—said, Lord what
wilt thou have me to do? He was now completely yielded. He was acknowledging this Lord to be his Lord with
the right to direct him. The Lord had a servant in Damascus whom He would use to lead Saul to the next step in
his new life. The Lord said, Arise, and go into the city. He would go on to Damascus, but under different
circumstances. He did not know what was next, but he was ready and obedient. Saul was not saved yet, but
godly sorrow and conviction were doing their work on him. The other men of the company stood speechless—
astonished also—hearing a voice, but seeing no man. They heard the voice but did not distinguish it as the
voice of the Lord. We can relate to this in our worship services. When the spirit of conviction is sent in a
powerful way, loud and clear, some tremble under conviction for their sins while others do not recognize it as
the voice of Jesus giving invitation to a rich life in salvation.
On to Damascus
Acts 9:8-9 Saul arose . . . he saw no man: but they led him. He was blinded by the heavenly light. In
Damascus, he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink —a real fast. A real burden of
conviction will take away some desires, both natural appetites and unnatural ones. Real conviction causes some
to stop smoking, drinking, and other things even before they are saved. They spend time in prayer because
serious conviction is working on them.
Saul was a sinner, a murderer, a hater of Christ, and a persecutor of His people. What happened to Saul?
Later, explaining the change in his life, he always pointed to this experience on the road as the beginning of a
permanent change that lasted all of his life. There is but one explanation of such a change—the new birth. Saul
was on his way to new birth—to be born of the Spirit, made alive in Christ. Saul was not yet saved, but he was
on his way. He had a great start; now he must follow in obedience, step by step, the leading of God. In the next
lesson, we learn of his conversion.
JUST A THOUGHT
Confession is turning the heart inside out,
putting the sins out where they can be washed away.
