LESSON 2
SAUL'S CONVERSION
Scripture Text: Acts 9:10-22
In the last lesson we learned: Persecution of saints is persecution of
Jesus. Jesus sometimes speaks from Heaven to people on earth. A
sinner's life, rebelling against the Truth, is a hard conflict. Saul yielded
to God, and God led him. Hunger for God can be stronger than hunger
for food.
God knows His servants. When He has a work to be done, He puts
His hand upon one. He had Ananias at Damascus in the lesson today.
Ananias was listening and received a blessing as well as Saul.
Sometimes God looks and finds no man. When He needs you and me,
will He find us faithful? Or will a work go undone, a soul unsaved,
because we were not listening?
MEMORY VERSE: And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.
—Acts 9:20
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 61 Good tidings of salvation.
Tue.—Isaiah 65:1-7 A rebellious people.
Wed—Isaiah 53:1-12 Believe the Gospel.
Thu.—Romans 2:1-11 No respect of persons.
Fri.—1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 Spreading the Gospel.
Devotional Reading: Romans 10:11-21 Salvation for all.
God Instructs Ananias
Acts 9:10-14 There was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias. He was one God could use. The
Lord appeared to him in a vision and told him to go into the street . . . called Straight, to the house of Judas,
to Saul, of Tarsus: for behold, he prayeth. All with a desire to meet Jesus must be willing to go to Straight
Street. Saul had also been given a vision. He was shown beforehand the name of the man and what he would do.
Thus both Ananias and Saul were prepared for meeting. God's work is perfect. Ananias answered, Lord, I
have heard by many of this man. Saul's reputation was well known among the saints. Ananias questioned the
wisdom of meeting with Saul. The evil he had done to the saints at Jerusalem frightened them when they knew
he had come to do the same—to bind all that call on thy name—Jesus' name.
A Chosen Vessel
Acts 9:15-16 The Lord said . . . Go thy way. Jesus knew all about Saul. He wanted Ananias to do as told.
He explained, he is a chosen vessel unto me. He was to carry Jesus' name to kings, Gentiles, and Israelites. But
there were great things he must suffer for the sake of Jesus' name. Christ spoke to Ananias by name.
Christianity is a personal matter. God deals with us as individuals. The God who notes the fall of a sparrow
knows His children by name. Sometimes we do not like the tasks to which God commissions us, yet we find
later that they are the very things we would want most to do if we knew how it would end. Here Ananias was
guiding into the church the most influential saint that the church has known through the centuries.

Saul Becomes a Brother
Acts 9:17-18 Convinced, Ananias obeyed. The meeting was a loving, tender experience. Conviction had
finished its softening work on Saul. He had counted the cost and was ready to pay the price. Ananias put his
hands on Saul, calling him Brother Saul. It must have thrilled Saul's heart. Ananias came in the name of the
Lord Jesus and said Jesus sent him. That was his authority. It was also the bond of love between them. The
kindly greeting of Ananias and the tenderness of his touch must have convinced Saul that Christians were
different from any group of people he had ever dealt with before. He came that Saul might receive . . . sight—a
physical blessing—and be filled with the Holy Ghost—a spiritual blessing. Immediately the likeness of scales
fell from his eyes. On the road his thinking had been changed. For three days he had been counting the cost,
praying, yielding all to God, and asking for His directions. As Ananias spoke with him, his faith leaped up and
took hold. His heart was open to receive Christ. Now his heart was changed also. His burden of guilt was gone.
He was a new man. He arose, and was baptized. Saul did not draw back. He bore witness to all by this symbol
of death to sin and new life in Christ that had been accomplished in his heart. Saul turned from misguided zeal
and adhering to dead religion and following the customs of men and became an Apostle of Christ. His soul was
healed. He was no longer the cruel enemy of any man; he was the loving servant of all.
Saul Bears Fruit
Acts 9:19-20 His burden of sin gone, Saul took food, he was strengthened. He stayed a time with the
disciples . . . at Damascus, fellowshipping, learning, rooting in this new soil, and growing. He was not only
taking in, he was giving out. Straightway—without waiting—he preached Christ . . . that he is the Son of
God—the Truth he had not believed, but which now gripped his soul. He preached it in the synagogues—just
where he had intended to destroy Christ's name. The letters in his pocket empowered him to punish those who
called on that name. The Spirit in his heart empowered him to proclaim it. The Spirit had won his heart and
made the letters useless.
Saul began to preach at once. Who licensed him? What school trained him? What church was he a member
of? God had made him a member of His church, placed him, and enabled him to preach. God gave him authority
and controlled him through His Spirit. Nothing more was necessary. Nothing more is necessary for anyone.
Education is good, but it is not enough. Human joining and control are not good.
A Different Saul
Acts 9:21-22 All that heard him were amazed—an unbelievable change. Is not this he that destroyed ...?
Yes, the same, yet no, not the same—transformed by Jesus Christ. Saul increased the more in strength—grew
in grace—proving that this is the very Christ—the One anointed to be the Savior, the One God promised to
send, the Son of God.
JUST A THOUGHT
No title a human being can hold carries greater honor than "Brother."

LESSON 3
PAUL BEGINS HIS MINISTRY
Scripture Text: Acts 9:23-31
Saul, later named Paul, successfully proved Jesus' deity to the Jews at
Damascus. Not wanting to believe this, they were greatly angered. In
Galatians 1:15-18 Paul tells us that following his conversion, he went into
Arabia. He went to commune with God and meditate that he might rightly
understand the Truth of the Gospel which had been revealed to him and
which he was to preach. Then he returned again unto Damascus. The three
years of verse 18 probably cover his stay in Arabia and his preaching in
Damascus.
Paul's taking of his teaching of Christ's deity from Damascus to the
Jewish synagogue brought great opposition and persecution. We reap as
we sow. Barnabas was a loving Christian brother.
MEMORY VERSE: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of
season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
—2 Timothy 4:2
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Romans 8:28-39 More than conquerors.
Tue.—Ephesians 3:8-21 According to eternal purpose.
Wed.—2 Timothy 1:7-14 Called with a holy calling.
Thu.—1 Peter 1:10-23 Be holy in conduct.
Fri.—Ephesians 1:3-14 Chosen to be holy.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 24:3-14 Endure to the end.
Paul Escapes Danger
Acts 9:23-25 Paul took his teaching of Christ's deity to the point of greatest opposition, the Jewish
synagogue. After many days this brought great persecution. The Jews took counsel to kill him. Determined to
accomplish this end, they watched the gates day and night. Paul knew this. It must have been a frightening
game of hide-and-seek until Paul's brethren took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket. As
Paul quickly climbed out of the basket in the dark and started the long trip to Jerusalem (some one hundred sixty
miles), he must have been thinking of times when he had been the persecutor rather than the persecuted. He was
reaping what he had sowed. While he patiently reaped, he was sowing better seed for a joyous reaping that is
even now continuing.
Paul at Jerusalem
Acts 9:26-28 Paul came back to Jerusalem a different man than left. He is one of the clearest examples we
have of the Truth that if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17). Reaching
Jerusalem, Paul assayed to join himself to the disciples—tried to fellowship with them. He was one of them
now. But they were all afraid—they knew his former activity among them. They believed this to be some kind
of trick, what we would call infiltration today. But Barnabas lovingly brought him to the apostles, told of his
experience with the Lord and his preaching at Damascus. They were convinced. They accepted Paul, and he
was with them coming in and going out—moved with them freely.

Yes, Paul was a changed man. The change in him was more evident because of the public character of his
wickedness and later of his preaching. Yet every redeemed soul is as much a new creature. If one is not a new
being, there has been no new birth. When the sinner dies and the saint is born, the life has a new Source, new
Master, new purposes and loves, and a new destiny.
We discern the character of Barnabas in the fact that when no one else had any faith in Saul's sincerity and
testimony, he trusted him and went out of his way to help him. There was no man to whom Paul owed so much
as he did to his loving brother, Barnabas. Since Paul was to mean so much to Christianity through the ages, the
part Barnabas played in bridging the gap between Paul and the Apostles and the church was a bright jewel in his
crown of Christian service.
Brethren Concerned
Acts 9:29-30 Paul, coming in and going out, spoke boldly—it took courage—in the name of the Lord
Jesus. One purpose filled his life now, and by God's grace, he kept busy at it. He disputed against the
Grecians—foreign Jews or proselytes brought in from outside. Paul preached boldly in spite of danger. His
strong preaching of Jesus as the Son of God angered them. They, like the Damascus Jews, went about to slay
him. The brethren—men of the church—found out the plan. They were more concerned than Paul for himself.
They brought him . . . to Caesarea, and sent him forth to Tarsus, his home.
Rest for a Season
Acts 9:31 Then had the churches—local congregations—rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and
Samaria—all of Palestine west of the Jordan River. With the chief contender out of the country, the Jew's anger
cooled somewhat, and they ceased for a time to harass the church. The church could now give unhindered
attention to prayer, worship, study, teaching, and service. Therefore, they were edified. They walked in the fear
of the Lord—carefully obeying—and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost—the inner blessings the Holy Spirit
bestowed. They were multiplied—souls were saved and added to the church. It was a time of spiritual
prosperity. Their greatest strength was in the fact of the Spirit's presence in each one. They walked with sins
forgiven in the comfort of the Holy Ghost. A Spirit-filled church bears spiritual fruit and wins souls.
Gospel preaching is not to be silenced because of opposition or the noisy clamor of the world. Persecution
and peace can each be used of God to bless the church. We should watch for opportunities to help, encourage,
and exalt a brother or sister. What can we learn here that will help us individually?
JUST A THOUGHT
As scarce as Truth is, the supply has always exceeded the demand.

HEALING AND RAISING THE DEAD
Scripture Text: Acts 9:32-43
After Paul's departure for Tarsus, the Jerusalem church enjoyed a
period of quiet and freedom, prospering spiritually and in numbers.
Peter went throughout all quarters contacting the saints, getting
together for spiritual talk, prayer, and exhortation. This is good. It
encourages, strengthens, and builds us up. Doing so, we grow in grace
and knowledge and skill in God's work. Paul wrote to forsake not the
assembling of ourselves together, but to exhort one another (Hebrews
The lesson today sets forth a number of important truths. One is that
God often chooses people of low estate, according to worldly standards,
to fulfill some important work. Dorcas was not a person of high position. She appears to have had neither wealth
nor learning. She was skilled in sewing and had a deep concern in her heart for the poor. Because of this, God
used her to do a great work in His kingdom.

—Acts 9:42

Aeneas Healed
Acts 9:32-35 Peter passed throughout all quarters. He went out from Jerusalem to visit the churches,
probably evangelizing as he went. He came . . . to the saints . . . at Lydda. There he found Aeneas, bedfast
eight years with palsy —paralysis. We would call it a hopeless case. Peter said . . . Aeneas, Jesus Christ
maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. He could not do this in his unhealed condition. He did not
question the fact that he had not done this for eight years; he arose immediately—no hesitation. This was proof
of his healing. All that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him—everyone was present and all saw the miracle—
and turned to the Lord. Many souls were saved.
When God works miracles and the church acts as pleases Him, people are awakened by the nearness and
power of God. They are convinced, realizing this is the God they have offended and the God they need. God
does the same now as then.

about it, write about it, or preach about it; Dorcas performed it. She was sick, and died. They washed her and

Many believed in the Lord. It is not what we have that counts in God's sight or how much we give. His interest

Dorcas had a place in the Kingdom of God, you and I have a place. As her humble gifts were helpful in God's
work, ours will be. But let us be sure we have the compassionate heart of Dorcas and her loving faith in Christ.
Then our works will be good works as hers were.

The temple of God must be richly adorned—the temple of the heart.

CORNELIUS' VISION
Scripture Text: Acts 10:1-8
We have followed Peter from Lydda to Joppa on his tour visiting the
saints. Today we meet a new brother and learn of an experience he had
that leads Peter on to the next point.
This lesson teaches us that in the early church there was neither racial
nor social intolerance. It is a good lesson on putting first the work that
needs to be done for God, and second, any personal ambition one may
entertain.
There is a very striking analogy between radio reception and the
spiritual reception that we experience when our receiving set, the human
heart, is tuned in perfectly to the Spirit and purposes of God. Peter had
more than just a new message; he had a new Gospel to carry, and the Lord wanted him to carry it everywhere.
God directed him.
MEMORY VERSE: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
—John 10:27

Mon.—Ephesians 2:1-13 Delivered from the world.
Tue.—Isaiah 40:25-31 The everlasting God.

Cornelius Prayed
Acts 10:1-2 Caesarea was the headquarters of the Roman Army in Judaea. A band was three to six hundred
soldiers and was divided into six centuries of one hundred soldiers each. Each century was commanded by a
centurion (Smith's Bible Dictionary).
Cornelius was a centurion of . . . the Italian band, volunteers from Italy. He was a Gentile or non-Jew. He
was devout to what he knew—he feared God, but had never met him personally—gave much alms to the
people—probably the poor and needy. He prayed to God alway. He was in condition to hear God speak. He
realized his best was not good enough.
Cornelius Sees a Vision
Acts 10:3-6 He saw in a vision . . . the ninth hour—mid-afternoon. He was fasting and praying at the time
(see verse 30). He saw . . . an angel of God . . . Saying . . . Cornelius . . . he was afraid. What is it, Lord? He
was ready to listen. Thy prayers and thine alms are come . . . before God. God had heard and seen. His
prayer had made an impression on God at the throne of grace. God hears and answers the prayer of sinners when
it concerns their salvation, the saving of their souls. This was His answer. For a memorial—a remembrance—
he was in ready condition to receive something that would be stamped on the memory of both God and
Cornelius.

Standing out in this account of Cornelius is the fact of the rulership of the Holy Spirit. Man was not directing
the actions of the individuals. No, it was the Lord, an angel of God or the Spirit Who spoke to them. It is
important that we understand what state of spiritual life Cornelius was in at the time of this lesson and the next.
He was devout, a just man, but he did not yet have salvation from sin. He desired something in his life that
which he needed to fill the void he felt in his soul. That something was freedom from sin through salvation that
only Jesus could provide.
What if Cornelius had been careless or self-willed or set on worldly thoughts? He would have missed God's
voice. God was drawing him. He hungered and thirsted after righteousness, and God understood what he could
not put into words. Jesus promises that such people will be filled (Matthew 5:6).
Cornelius Obeys
Acts 10:7-8 Cornelius believed God; he lost no time. He called two of his household servants, and a
devout soldier. He declared all and sent them to Joppa. He highly trusted them.
Soldiers are not generally known for goodness. Yet, Cornelius had several around him who seemed to share
his interest in the things of God. He felt he could trust them with his precious story and with carrying out his
command. They showed no negative tendencies toward their mission. All his house feared God. This is a great
testimony to the good character of Cornelius in regard to the position he held. It would appear he had a good
influence upon his household. Possibly one of them had influenced him for God. Whichever, this is a genuine
influence for God. We should have a burden for the spreading of the good news of the Gospel to those around us
and especially to those of our own family.
It is a precious privilege to be a tool for God to use. We should praise God that He stoops to use humans to
do His work of spreading the Gospel and building His church. This draws all concerned into close unity with
each other and with Him. Cornelius heard Jesus' voice and obeyed. Jesus saw into his heart and knew him for
what he was. This resulted in much good.

The religious plane upon which we live is setting the standard for someone else.

PETER'S VISION
Scripture Text: Acts 10:9-23
There was a road along the coast of Samaria that ran from Joppa to Caesarea.
Last Sunday we stood at the Caesarea end of that road and looked at the vision God
sent to Cornelius. Today we stand at the Joppa end and look at another vision. The
visions are a pair. Together they caused two men to meet and change history. This
would lead to the first Gentile being born into the church. Peter seems not to have
laid out a schedule. He seems to have waited for God's direction of where to go and
when.
God's plans are always in perfect order. When He told Cornelius to send for Peter, He prepared Peter to go.
When He commands us, He makes the way before us. God knows the end. We can trust Him. What God
commands, we can do without question. The law of clean and unclean animals is removed.

not thou common.
—Acts 10:15

The Vision of Peter
Acts 10:9-10 On the morrow—the day after Cornelius' vision and starting of men to contact Peter—as
they—the men—went . . . and drew nigh to Joppa, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth
hour—noon, dinnertime. Peter was hungry. (God wanted Peter hungry to receive the vision.) Peter fell into a
trance—a state in which the soul seems carried away or absorbed in a vision.
Waiting time need not be wasted time. We are told to be redeeming the time. Parts of time some might waste
in jesting, gossip, watching demoralizing TV, or pursuing wrong goals. Waiting time may be used in study,
prayer, edifying talk, rest of the body, or purposeful tasks. Thus they may add up to real accomplishment for the
Lord. Peter used his wait to pray. Doing so, he put himself at God's disposal and opened the door for the vision
he could have missed by wrong use of his time.
Acts 10:11-13 Peter saw a vessel like a sheet caught up at the corners descending from Heaven to Earth. In
it were all manner of . . . beasts . . . and creeping things, and fowls. A voice said, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.
Peter needed food. Here was food. But Peter's belief stood in the way. God's Law forbade eating unclean flesh
(Leviticus 11). Some of these animals were unclean.
Why did God give this Law and later set it aside? As all of the Law, He gave it to bring mankind to Christ
(Galatians 3:23-25). The Law was a type, a forerunner of something better to come. Christ was the fulfillment
of it. Read Colossians 2:8-17; Romans 14:14; Hebrews 8:8-13. By the Law of clean and unclean foods, God
taught people to put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean (Leviticus 10:10;
Leviticus 20:25-26). Salvation in Jesus provides us a better Law. The food Law has no further use.

Call Not Thou Common
Acts 10:14-16 Peter said, Not so, Lord. Peter always quick to answer back did not realize he was
contradicting God. This was a learning experience for him. God was bringing forth new Laws in a new
dispensation. Now the same God Who gave the Law was giving Peter another command that took away the first.
What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. If God made the unclean animals clean, they were
clean. Peter was to accept them as clean. This was done thrice. The whole vision came three times to
emphasize it. The lesson is true, clear, and for us all.
As the Law on food had a temporary use, so the rejection of Gentiles was temporary. It had set Israel aside
for a time in preparation for Christ's coming. Now God puts no difference between any people. For the same
Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him (Romans 10:12). As some cling to the outmoded Law of
unclean foods, so some hold some people as beneath them. It is wrong to consider any class of people as
common or unclean. Anyone can be saved as well as us.
What Was Its Meaning?
Acts 10:17-22 While Peter doubted in himself—wondered, meditated, pondered—what this vision . . .
should mean, he felt it had greater meaning than about the animals only. Just then the men . . . from Cornelius
. . . stood before the gate and inquired for Peter. While Peter thought on the vision, the Spirit said . . . men
seek thee. The Spirit could talk to Peter and straighten out his thinking. Peter met the three men and was told of
Cornelius' vision. The Spirit told him to go with the men, doubting nothing—without further question, sure that
it was right to do so—for I have sent them. Now Peter understood the vision: Cornelius was a Gentile. Peter, a
Jew, believed that the Israelite nation was chosen by God as a peculiar treasure unto Him above all people
(Exodus 19:5-6). He believed salvation was for Jews only. He had believed it would be wrong to take it to the
Gentiles, as they were "unclean" people, or rejected by God. Now the vision taught him that as all flesh was
cleansed and fit for food, so all people were included in the offer of salvation. Christ died for ALL. Peter was to
call no man common or unclean.
Peter's Obedience
Acts 10:23 God had sent the men, and Peter was glad to obey. After lodging the men overnight, Peter went
away with them, accompanied by certain brethren from Joppa. What God commands, we can do without
question. The Spirit never directs contrary to God's Word.
JUST A THOUGHT
Those who deserve love least need it more.

SALVATION TO THE GENTILES

Cornelius invited friends and associates to hear the message from God.
Neither Peter nor any human is to be worshiped. All classes of people are to
be accepted on equal terms. Peter exalted Jesus Christ. We should learn from
this lesson that the sectarian walls built between saints are wrong. What God
accepts, we should accept.
How deep is the experience of one who is not concerned for the salvation
of those near him? When God has control of a heart, He reaches out from that heart to others. God is love.
Concern for others is necessary if we are to win them to Christ.

Cornelius and Peter Meet

God Is No Respecter of Persons
Acts 10:34-35 Peter . . . said . . . God is no respecter of persons. Here it is, the Truth about human

PETER'S RESPONSE TO HIS BRETHREN

Sometimes one has not only to carry out a project, but also to defend his
action before those who question it. Such was Peter's experience after he
went to Cornelius. Sometimes when our action is questioned by our
brethren, we are tempted to be resentful and belligerent. It is better to
assume that the critics are also desirous of doing God's will and keeping the
church clean.
Those in the lesson today were. Peter kindly but frankly explained. Very
recently he had held the same attitude as these brethren now held. He treated
them with the same understanding God had used in teaching him. Let us look at the result as recorded in this
lesson.

Points in Peter's Defense
Acts 11:12-17 The Spirit bade me go. (1) Peter's action was not of his own planning. It was obedience to
God's Spirit. These brethren had the Spirit and understood Peter. These six brethren accompanied me. (2) He
had witnesses. They witnessed the happening, agreed with no objection. (3) Peter briefly told of Cornelius'
vision, which agreed with his own. Call for Simon—Peter—who shall tell thee words whereby thou . . . shall
be saved. Forasmuch then—since—God gave them the like gift—the Holy Spirit, as he did to us. (4) They
had obtained the gift the same way. They believed on the Lord Jesus Christ; what was I, that I could
withstand God? (5) Peter pointed out his lack of authority in this. The act was God's, not his. Only God can
send the Holy Spirit. (6) Peter plead his responsibility to God. Since God is perfect and all-powerful, Peter had
no right to question His acts, only to cooperate with Him. God, Who made, at first, the distinction between Jews
and Gentiles, has a right to remove it, whenever and by whatever means He pleases. Peter saw both Jews and
Gentiles going to Heaven.
The Apostles' Conclusion
Acts 11:18 These brethren were servants of God; they were Apostles. Peter, a short time ago, had felt and
believed as they. They did not have the authority to decide this among themselves. It did not rest in them to
make rules and creeds and doctrines, to legislate for the church. They were not a governing body. That authority
is God's alone. They were only servants to carry out the commands of Christ as the Spirit directed. When they
heard these things, they held their peace—had nothing to say. They dropped all contention and glorified
God—praised and thanked Him. They yielded to God's decision. They accepted those whom God accepted.
They decided according to facts, not prejudice. They agreed that God had granted repentance unto life to the
Gentiles.
How About Us?
The people at Caesarea had been saved by way of repentance. They did not join anything. They came in by
the door, the new birth, which gave them life in Christ. God added them to the church. There is no other way to
get in.
Prejudice and customs are hard to give up. We do not like to change an opinion long held or to break the
common-belief bond with friends. But the operation of the Holy Spirit in the heart can change the mind also. He
gives one a love for God's will above all else. These saints had the Holy Spirit. He gave them a childlike
sincerity. Learning God's will meant for them the dropping of contrary opinions and brought a rejoicing in the
Truth. We should judge by facts, not by what we hear. We should rejoice in the salvation of others. How about
you, dear friend?
JUST A THOUGHT
There is plenty of heavenly music for those who are tuned in.

THE CHURCH SCATTERED BY

The persecution of the brethren following the death of Stephen
scattered the saints far and wide, and so, instead of extinguishing the fire
of the new faith, succeeded only in spreading it. Now they were
conscious that the Gospel was meant for all men everywhere. Now all
nations could receive the Christian faith. Here we notice that God does
great things through plain, ordinary, humble people. We observe, also,
that evangelism sometimes begins not in public meeting but in private
conversation.

them under the direction of the Spirit gave this church leadership, administered in love and brotherhood, not in
dominion and authority. Today we get a look at the scattering of these saints and the result of their witness.

the Lord.

Barnabas Sent to Investigate
Acts 11:22-24 The church in Jerusalem, hearing of the evangelization of Greeks, sent Barnabas. He was also
from Cyprus (4:36). He was to go as far as Antioch. In Antioch Barnabas saw the grace of God—it was God's
work, these people had the real goods. He was glad. No objection from him. He rejoiced in the Truth. He
exhorted them to cleave unto the Lord—to continue holding fast to Jesus. They should do it with purpose of
heart—determination, from the heart pressing on to the goal set before them. Barnabas was a good man.
Barnabas partook of this quality of God because God was in him. He was full of the Holy Ghost and of faith.
While he was in Antioch, much people was added unto the Lord—were saved.
The Jerusalem church seems to have exercised leadership in the activities. This does not mean it held
superior rights of authority or was a governing body. We see brotherly concern, investigation and advice, but no
rulership. The rulership of the Holy Spirit is very evident as we move through our study. The Apostles had
associated with Jesus in Jerusalem; they had greater experience than most others had. Since the Holy Spirit came
first in Jerusalem, they had more time to become established. The Apostles at Jerusalem, as human instruments,
had been given the Spirit's gifts and knew how to use them. If we are faithful where we happen to be and wait
patiently upon the Lord, He will move us into greater areas of service when we are ready for them.
Barnabas Brings Paul
Acts 11:25-26 Then Barnabas went to Tarsus for to seek Saul. When he had found him—It is apparent
that he had to look for him, remembering that Tarsus was Paul's home, where they had sent him for safety (Acts
9:30). Now the loving heart of Barnabas wanted Paul to enjoy these good meetings at Antioch and the newly
saved to benefit from Paul's clear teaching. He brought him unto Antioch, where for a year they both taught
much people. The disciples were called Christians first in Antioch—like Christ, followers of Christ. People
must have seen a resemblance strong enough to warrant the name. Do they see that resemblance in us?
Barnabas did not forget Paul. He had brought Paul to the church at first (Acts 9:27). His action then in
bringing Paul into fellowship with the church there, and now bringing him back into active duty, may be the
connecting link which gave the world the great service of the Apostle Paul.
Let us take this opportunity to stir up our minds in way of remembrance of what it means to be a follower of
Christ. It means, first of all, to follow Christ in His teachings. These teachings are contrary to the teachings of
the world. Once we have decided to be followers of Christ, we have to bid goodbye to the world's ways and
walk the road Christ walked. This He teaches through His Word. Read and study it. The Bible is the Christian's
road map.
Antioch Christians Believed the Prophets
Acts 11:27-30 Came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch. Prophets deliver to the people whatever
message God gives them. One, Agabus, was given forecasts of the future. (Acts 21:10-11). He told them by the
Spirit—not his own judgment— that great dearth—scarcity, want, lack of food on account of crop failure—
was coming throughout all the world. The Antioch disciples believed the message. They determined to send
relief to the church in Judaea. Each gave voluntarily and according to his ability. This is God's way. They
chose Barnabas and Saul to carry the offering to Jerusalem to the elders for distribution.

AN ANGEL IN PRISON
Scripture Text: Acts 12:1-19
In our last lesson we learned of a famine in Judaea. The church in
Antioch sent money and food to the church in Jerusalem, and Paul and
Barnabas were selected to take it.
About this time Herod began a new persecution of the church and killed
James, the brother of John. Seeing it pleased the Jews, he put Peter in
prison, but the church prayed for him continually. The night before Herod
was to bring him forth for trial, the angel of the Lord appeared in the prison
and caused the chains to fall off Peter's ankles and led Peter out of the
prison and set him free. Peter went to the home of Mary, the mother of John
Mark, where the church was gathered praying.
In our lesson today we learn that we should spread the Gospel of Christ
in spite of persecution. We should pray, expecting God to answer, even to
bring miracles. We must not question God's wisdom and judgment. The
thing of greatest importance is that God's program goes forward.

—Jeremiah 32:27

Persecution by Herod
Acts 12:1-3 About that time—when Barnabas and Saul brought the relief gifts from Antioch to
Jerusalem—Herod began to vex certain of the church. The church had enjoyed a period of rest from
persecution, but it did not last. Herod Agrippa I was king of Judaea, Samaria, and other parts. He was a strict

The church was making great progress throughout the land. Opposition brought persecution. Seeing the death of

Peter's release. Peter knocked. Rhoda was so surprised that she failed to open the door, but ran to tell. The
surprise was so great that the others did not believe her at first. Thou art mad—insane. Then, as Rhoda insisted

had done.
Sixteen soldiers suffered death unjustly. This is part of God's plan in both the Old Testament and the New.
God's program has often brought death or suffering to some, as the slaughter of babies at Jesus' coming
(Matthew 2:16), the death of people and animals in the Flood (Genesis 7:21-22), and the loss of swine at the
healing of the demon-possessed man (Mark 5:11-13). Why? Because of the influence of sin. God's program is
not inferior, that it should wait on the convenience of every cause. It must be carried on. He will not allow any
power to stand in His way of progress. It is not ours to question His judgment. Tragedies occur because it is a
sinful world, not because God desires them. God's program will go forward. Can He use you?

HEROD'S DESTRUCTION
Scripture Texts: Acts 12:19-25; Proverbs 6:16-17
Herod, King of Judaea, Samaria, and other dominions of Rome, had been
persecuting the church at Jerusalem. He had killed James and imprisoned Peter.
God miraculously rescued Peter.
How much we sometimes pay for worthless trifles in this life. In our lesson
we are told of people who gave honor to Herod, but it was only lip service offered
to gain favor for them. It was empty flattery. It was wrong. Yet for receiving this
blasphemous praise of the people, he paid his soul. We see the result of pride in
the heart of man.
MEMORY VERSE: Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name.
—1 Chronicles 16:29a

Tue.—Romans 12:1-10 Careful of conduct.

Seeking Herod's Favor
Acts 12:19-20 Not finding his prisoner, Peter, Herod ordered the keepers executed. Then, leaving bereaved
hearts behind him, he went down to Caesarea, where was his official residence. Herod was highly displeased
with them of Tyre and Sidon, cities farther north along the coast. They came to him from there, used the clever
strategy of first making friends with Blastus, Herod's chamberlain, then worked up to desire peace with the king
himself. This was not because they admired Herod or desired his personal friendship. It was because their
country was nourished by the king's country. It was for their own selfish advantage, for their economic
welfare. As saints, we must never join hands with the world for any personal benefit or gain.
Herod's Oration
Acts 12:21-22 Upon a set day—arranged and announced—Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his
throne—with all the power of state and much pomp and show—made an oration—an elaborate public
discourse treating an important subject in a formal and dignified manner. The people gave a shout—applause.
The praise was personal and the very highest. It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. It was not sincere, it
was flattery, designed to win Herod's favor for themselves. It was blasphemy. It was wrong for them to give and
wrong for Herod to accept. Raising any person or thing to the place of God is idolatry. It is wrong to take glory
to ourselves. All glory belongs to God, but Herod took it to himself. To speak words of thanks and appreciation
to our brethren for a good work is not giving them God's glory. This is part of the debt of love we owe them.
Here is a man, a strict keeper of the Law ceremonies, raised to political power and honor, bound by sin,
trying to rise on false glory to a place of godliness. He was building on a false foundation which would not hold,
and he fell. His house was built on the sand. When it fell, as all such must, great was the fall of it. Read
Galatians 6:3. Look not with scorn. Look not with self-righteousness, thinking it could not happen to you.

Herod's Punishment
Acts 12:23 Immediately—usually the bulk of sin's punishment is deferred, but it is always certain, unless
forgiven. The angel of the Lord smote him. Angels are God's servants, sent sometimes to bless, sometimes to
punish. God punished Herod's sin at once. Why? Because he gave not God the glory. He accepted the
blasphemous praise of the people. He took it as being due him. He did not refuse it and pass it on to God. He
gave up the ghost—destroyed physically and spiritually. He paid with his soul.
We are not kings. Most of us do not make orations to a nation. But there is a danger facing all of us. Herod's
trouble did not start in what he did. It lay deeper. He had much pride and self-righteousness and arrogance in his
heart. The capacity for pride seems overgrown in human nature. It lies in every unregenerate heart (Mark 7:21-
23). It is easily revived by success or praise. To see the ever-threatening danger, look at the number of sad
wrecks it is causing. Often a talented, promising one lets success "go to his head" and falls from usefulness, a
victim to pride. We can be proud of something or proud of nothing, proud of our pride or proud of our humility.
Whatever the form, it is still pride. Pride in the heart is sin (Proverbs 21:4).
The Sin of Pride
Proverbs 6:16-17 These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: A
proud look . . . (See also Proverbs 8:13.) Pride is selfish. It is desire for glory. It is an overvaluation of the
esteem of one's self. It is a lust of the flesh, and is not of the Father (1 John 2:16). All glory and honor belong
to God (Psalm 115:1). To take any upon ourselves is stealing from Him. All the good that we have comes from
Him.
The Remedy for Pride
Jesus' warning to watch needs to be diligently obeyed in the area of pride. Many saved ones have been lost
over this temptation, blindly going on thinking themselves rich, when really they are wretched, and miserable,
and poor, and blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17-18). This need not be. Jesus stands ready to save to the
uttermost. He asks us to buy of Him gold tried in the fire, real, spiritual riches. He will lift you out of the mire
of sin to His plane of salvation. He will cleanse the heart of pride, arrogance, and every defilement. Jesus Christ
is the only remedy.
Success of the Gospel Continued
Acts 12:24-25 But the word of God grew and multiplied. This is not a change of subject. The conjunction
but connects it with what went before, connects it in contrast. Herod had set out to destroy the Gospel by killing
its promoters. He has gone down in defeat, while the Gospel lives and grows. Barnabas and Saul returned
from Jerusalem to Antioch, when they had fulfilled their ministry of delivering the gift from the Antioch
church to the church in Judaea. They took with them John Mark as they continued the spread of the Gospel of
Jesus Christ. Fighting against the power of the Gospel is a losing battle.
JUST A THOUGHT
Never forget that the way up is down.

The Devil Opposes Truth
Acts 13:6-8 At Paphos was a sorcerer and false prophet named Elymas. He was with a man of high position.

His Truth. It claims to heal and tell fortunes and reveal secret wisdom by the power of God's Spirit, but really
works by the spirits of devils. Sorcery or spiritism is dangerous. Revelation 21:8 tells the end of sorcerers.
Elymas was a false prophet, one who claimed to have a divine commission to speak in God's name. But God

promised made prophets and teachers. It gave Paul discernment to understand the character of Elymas and to
pronounce blindness upon him, and to teach and win the deputy.

returned home. He was young, this life was physically hard, and perhaps he was homesick. Later, he proved to
be a good worker (2 Timothy 4:11).

PROGRESS IN GOD'S KINGDOM

Him and His promise—are justified—cleared of guilt—from all things—all sins, saved to the uttermost.
Justification cannot be obtained by the law of Moses. Paul had placed two methods of salvation opposite each
other. He said one was perfectly successful, the other a perfect failure. The method he called successful was
fiercely opposed by the Jews. The one he called a failure was that held by them. He warned them of the danger
of rejecting Christ, quoting Habakkuk 1:5 (verse 41). Their unbelief was prophesied long before.
Acts 13:42-43 There were many Gentiles in the audience who, because they believed in one God, had
accepted the Jewish faith. Many of the Gentiles remained after the meeting and asked for this preaching again
the next Sabbath. A good number of Jews and proselytes believed. They followed Paul and Barnabas, hungry
for spiritual food. The Apostles encouraged them to continue in the grace of God. The Apostles' advice to them
needs to be repeated over and over. Only those who endure unto the end will be finally saved (Matthew 24:13).
To endure, we must have grace. Grace is a supply of God's own life which He pours into the lives of His
children as we need it. To obtain it, stay in contact with God. Live in His strength, not yours.
The Jews followed the Law. Now the Law was fulfilled in Christ, but the Jews would not believe. They held
back for the old forms and symbols. These could never save them. If we think we can be justified by our
obedience to forms, by going to church, by baptism, by signing a card, by good works, etc., we are like the Jews.
We can be justified only by believing in Christ.
Opposition From the Jews
Acts 13:44-52 The next Sabbath day came almost the whole city—many gathered which excited envy in
the Jews. It widened the gap between them and the Gentiles. They opposed Paul's teaching, contradicting and
blaspheming. Paul boldly told them that the word of God was to be spoken to them first. He told them if they
rejected God's Word and everlasting life, we turn to the Gentiles. He recalled God's Words to him sending him
to the Gentiles and to take salvation unto the ends of the earth (Acts 9:15; Acts 22:15, Acts 22:21; Acts 26:16-
18). Gentiles believed and spread the Word to the ends of the earth. The Jews raised persecution and drove
out the Apostles, who left filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost. Acts 9:16 was beginning to be fulfilled in
Paul.
Paul saw issues clearly. He wanted others to. God, not men, taught Paul the Gospel (Galatians 1:11-12). He
presented it boldly to the very ones who would oppose it most. Many would fear to do so. Paul used no shallow
talk of all going to the same place, or all being children of God. He knew the deadly disease these people
suffered from. He knew the remedy that saved him. He knew from his experience that it would work. He laid it
plainly before the people. When they refused it, he was through with them because God was through with them.
They had judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life. By their words and conduct, they had passed
sentence upon themselves and, in effect, had stated that they were unworthy of the grace of the Gospel. The
Gospel was to them a savor of death unto death.
JUST A THOUGHT
A method of finding work to do is to make ourselves available to God
and wait for an opening and His leading.
